title: Rethinking the Legal Profession’s Role in Business and Human Rights
gist: After the Supreme Court's June 2026 Cisco v. Doe ruling closed Alien Tort Statute aiding-and-abetting liability, ABA and CSIS authors argue that Congress and the legal profession must fill the accountability gap on remedy, supply-chain due diligence and SLAPPs.

themes.theme: Cisco v. Doe and loss of U.S. remedy

insights.claim: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on June 23 in Cisco Systems v. Doe I that federal courts cannot create new causes of action under the Alien Tort Statute, so aiding-and-abetting liability falls outside it, closing the path to sue companies for helping others commit human rights abuses.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Materially lowers U.S. litigation risk for multinationals over foreign human rights abuses linked to their technology or services.
insights.quote: ruling 6–3 that federal courts cannot create new causes of action under the Alien Tort Statute

insights.claim: The Fourth Circuit has since read Cisco to foreclose judicially created ATS liability more broadly, ordering dismissal of claims by three Abu Ghraib detainees who had won a $42 million jury verdict in 2024.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shows the ruling's reach extends to existing large verdicts, cutting liability tail risk for defendants.

insights.claim: Cisco is the final step in a retreat through Kiobel (2013), Jesner (2018) and Nestle (2021), each of which narrowed the Alien Tort Statute.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Trend is one-directional; do not expect courts to restore corporate liability.

insights.claim: The ruling hits the third UNGP pillar, access to remedy, and removes a main way the U.S. legal system backed up the corporate responsibility to respect human rights without changing what the UNGPs expect of companies.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
insights.so_what: Expectations remain via European compliance regimes even as U.S. legal enforcement weakens.

insights.claim: Plaintiffs' counsel Paul Hoffman says it is now up to Congress to let victims of serious corporate human rights violations seek accountability in U.S. courts; the 2022 Alien Tort Statute Clarification Act (S. 4155) never received a vote and expired.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Legislative reversal is possible but has no near-term traction.

insights.claim: Apart from forced labor enforcement, the United States has no general requirement that companies identify and address human rights harm in their supply chains; advocates urge a Foreign Corrupt Practices Act for Human Rights and mandatory due diligence for federal contractors.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Contrasts with European due diligence mandates; a mandatory U.S. regime would raise compliance costs but is unlikely soon.

insights.claim: A properly staffed and empowered U.S. OECD National Contact Point is a voluntary, non-judicial route to remedy that cannot compel companies but would keep one avenue open when courts are closed; OECD Watch and more than 130 NGOs have called for strengthening such contact points.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reputational rather than legal exposure is where complaints will now be channeled.
insights.locator: A Properly Resourced U.S. OECD Contact Point

insights.claim: SLAPPs undercut due diligence because the activists, journalists and communities they target are often the source of the information due diligence depends on.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Suppressed signals mean companies and investors may underestimate supply-chain human rights risk.
insights.quote: Due diligence is hollowed out when the very voices that point to the abuse and the risks are silenced

insights.claim: The Free Speech Protection Act, introduced December 2024 by Senator Wyden and Representatives Raskin and Kiley, would let federal judges quickly dismiss speech-silencing suits and award fees; 34 states and D.C. have varying anti-SLAPP laws and federal circuits are split on applying them in diversity cases.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Patchwork state law leaves litigation-as-intimidation risk uneven.

insights.claim: Other tactics used to defend companies include burdensome discovery demands, threats of remedies a claimant is unlikely to obtain, settlement clauses that conceal evidence of ongoing harm, and cost demands to deter future plaintiffs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Opaque settlement terms can hide ongoing harm from investors.

insights.claim: With legislation unlikely to move soon, the profession's own rules, including ABA Model Rules 3, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.4(a) and ABA Resolution 604 (August 2024), are among the few remaining safeguards, and lawyers as advisers and advocates shape whether due diligence protects people or produces paperwork.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Legal sign-off alone is not evidence of effective human rights risk management.

insights.claim: Regulations that only penalize harm after the fact invite companies to price penalties in, whereas clear rules for every business let firms compete on how well they run operations, not on how little they spend on workers and communities.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Argues for ex-ante rules over penalties to avoid a race to the bottom.

top_entities: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
